passages.t: Sabbaths, New Moons and the way out
passages.happening:
The inner east gate is to be shut during the six working days, ‘but on the Sabbath day and on the day of the New Moon it shall be opened’ (verse 1). The prince is to enter through the porch of the gateway and stand by the gatepost while the priests offer his sacrifices; ‘He is to bow in worship at the threshold of the gate and then depart’ (verse 2). The people of the land bow at the entrance too (verse 3). Offerings for the Sabbaths and New Moons are listed (verses 4-8).

At the appointed feasts, ‘whoever enters by the north gate to worship must go out by the south gate’, and the reverse; ‘No one is to return through the gate by which he entered’ (verse 9). The prince goes in and out among the people (verse 10). Rules follow for grain offerings, freewill offerings and a daily burnt offering, morning by morning (verses 11-15).
passages.hearers:
The Sabbath and the New Moon were ancient holy days, often named together. Under the monarchy the king had a prominent role in temple worship, and some kings abused it; Uzziah was struck with leprosy for burning incense himself. Ezekiel's prince has a defined place: he stands at the gatepost, bows at the threshold and leaves. He never enters the inner court where the priests serve.

The rule about gates is partly crowd control on busy feast days. It may also carry a symbolic point: no one leaves God's presence the way they came in. The prince worships among the people, not apart from them.
passages.later: King Uzziah ‘entered the temple of the LORD to burn incense’ and was struck with a skin disease (2 Chronicles 26:16-19). The psalm says, ‘better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere’ (Psalm 84:10).
passages.asks: No one was to leave by the gate they came in. Ask whether worship changes you, or whether you leave the way you came. And ask what it would mean to walk out differently this week.

passages.t: The people's land, and the temple kitchens
passages.happening:
If the prince gives part of his inheritance to one of his sons, it stays in the family. If he gives it to a servant, it is his only ‘until the year of freedom; then it will revert to the prince’ (verse 17). ‘The prince must not take any of the inheritance of the people by evicting them from their property’ (verse 18), so that none of God's people will be scattered from their land.

Then the man showed Ezekiel the priests' kitchens, where they boil the guilt and sin offerings and bake the grain offering, so that they do not bring them into the outer court (verses 19-20). In the four corners of the outer court were kitchens with hearths. ‘These are the kitchens where those who minister at the temple will cook the sacrifices offered by the people’ (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The year of freedom draws on the Jubilee, the fiftieth year when land returned to its original families and Israelite servants went free. There is little evidence that it was regularly kept under the kings, and Jeremiah records how Jerusalem's leaders freed their slaves during the siege and then took them back. Ezekiel's rule protects ordinary families from losing their land to the ruler.

Worship at ancient temples was not quiet contemplation. It happened in open courts with crowds, animals, smoke and the smell of cooking. Many sacrifices were partly burned and partly eaten in a festive meal before God, which is why the temple needed kitchens.
passages.later: The law said, ‘proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants’ (Leviticus 25:10). Jerusalem's leaders freed their slaves and then took them back (Jeremiah 34:11).
passages.asks: The vision of God's house ends with kitchens, where the people's offerings were cooked and shared. Ask what it means that God's presence includes meals and ordinary work. And ask whom you could share a table with.
